skill.name: gget
skill.description: Guide bioinformatics work with gget for genomic database queries, sequence analysis, enrichment workflows, and reference data retrieval.
skill.summary: Use gget to query genomic databases and run common bioinformatics workflows.
skill.author: davila7

security_audit.summary: Most static findings are false positives from Markdown backticks, code fences, parameter documentation, URLs, or biological identifiers. Real concerns are unsafe credential examples, unconstrained output filenames, and pickle loading in a workflow example. No prompt injection attempt or malicious exfiltration intent was found.

remediation.issue: Credential examples place API keys or passwords on command lines.
remediation.suggestion: Replace command-line secret examples with secure setup guidance. Prefer environment variables, local credential stores, or interactive prompts that avoid shell history.

remediation.issue: FASTA-derived sequence IDs are used in output filenames without sanitization.
remediation.suggestion: Normalize sequence IDs to safe basenames. Reject path separators and verify resolved output paths remain inside the chosen output directory.

remediation.issue: The caching example loads pickle files without a trust warning.
remediation.suggestion: Use safer formats such as CSV, JSON, or Parquet for cache data. If pickle is required, document that only trusted cache files are safe.

remediation.issue: Examples download data and write many local outputs.
remediation.suggestion: Add guidance to use dedicated output directories, explicit limits, and licensing checks for large or credentialed database workflows.

semantic_findings.title: Command-Line Credential Exposure in Examples
semantic_findings.description: The COSMIC and GPT examples show credentials or API keys passed as command-line arguments. Users who copy this pattern can expose secrets through shell history, process listings, or shared logs.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The examples explicitly show --password and --api_key command-line usage. The values are placeholders, but the pattern encourages unsafe handling of real credentials.

semantic_findings.title: Untrusted FASTA Headers Used in Output Paths
semantic_findings.description: The batch sequence helper copies FASTA header text into output filenames. A crafted header containing path separators could write BLAST output outside the intended output directory.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The sequence ID is read directly from the FASTA header and later interpolated into a filename. No sanitization or path containment check is visible in the cited code.

semantic_findings.title: Unsafe Pickle Loading in Workflow Example
semantic_findings.description: The caching workflow uses pickle.load on a cache file path. Loading a pickle file from an untrusted location can execute arbitrary Python code.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The workflow directly loads pickle data when the cache file exists. The example does not state that cache files must be trusted or protected.

content.value_statement: Bioinformatics research often requires many database queries and file formats. This skill guides Claude, Codex, and Claude Code through gget commands and Python workflows.
actual_capabilities: Explain gget modules for gene search, sequence retrieval, BLAST, BLAT, and enrichment analysis.
Provide command-line and Python examples for common gget workflows.
Guide reference genome metadata lookup and Ensembl download options.
Describe disease, drug, expression, structure, and cancer genomics query workflows.
Use included helper scripts for gene analysis, enrichment analysis, and batch sequence analysis.
limitations: The skill depends on the installed gget package and its supported databases.
Many workflows require internet access to public scientific databases.
Some modules require large downloads or separate setup before use.
Database schemas and results may change as upstream providers update data.

use_cases.title: Investigate a Gene
use_cases.description: Find gene metadata, retrieve sequences, inspect expression, and review disease or drug associations.

use_cases.title: Prepare Sequence Workflows
use_cases.description: Run BLAST searches, align sequences, compare orthologs, and prepare structure prediction inputs.

use_cases.title: Build Reference Inputs
use_cases.description: List species, retrieve Ensembl reference metadata, and plan reproducible genome download commands.

prompt_templates.title: Find Gene Information
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the gget skill to find basic information for the gene TP53 in human. Include the best command-line and Python options.

prompt_templates.title: Retrieve Sequences
prompt_templates.prompt: Use gget to retrieve nucleotide and protein sequences for these Ensembl IDs: [paste IDs]. Save outputs with clear filenames.

prompt_templates.title: Analyze a Gene List
prompt_templates.prompt: Plan a gget enrichment workflow for this gene list: [paste genes]. Include ontology, pathway, and tissue expression checks.

prompt_templates.title: Design a Multi-Step Pipeline
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a reproducible gget pipeline for disease gene discovery, sequence retrieval, BLAST comparison, and result caching. Include safety checks.

output_examples.input: Ask for a quick TP53 gene analysis workflow.
output: Recommended gget search, info, sequence, expression, disease, and drug queries.
Expected output file names for metadata, FASTA sequences, expression tables, and association tables.
Notes about species naming, database updates, and result limits.

output_examples.input: Ask how to compare protein sequences across species.
output: A workflow that retrieves orthologs, obtains protein sequences, aligns sequences, and checks structures.
Suggested gget modules include bgee, seq, muscle, pdb, alphafold, and elm.
Warnings about AlphaFold setup, runtime, and large dependency downloads.

output_examples.input: Ask how to prepare reference files for RNA-seq analysis.
output: Steps to list species, select an Ensembl release, retrieve GTF and cDNA files, and record metadata.
Advice to store outputs in a dedicated directory and document release numbers.

best_practices: Use explicit species names, Ensembl releases, and result limits for reproducible queries.
Run large downloads and setup commands in a clean environment with enough storage.
Store API credentials outside prompts, shell history, notebooks, and shared files.
anti_patterns: Do not paste private API keys or database passwords into chat prompts.
Do not run large database downloads without checking disk space and licensing requirements.
Do not trust cached pickle files or FASTA headers from untrusted sources.

faq.question: What is gget used for?
faq.answer: gget queries genomic, protein, expression, disease, and structure databases from a command line or Python workflow.

faq.question: Does this skill install gget automatically?
faq.answer: No. It explains installation and usage, but the user controls package installation and setup commands.

faq.question: Which tools can use this skill?
faq.answer: The report lists support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.

faq.question: Does gget need internet access?
faq.answer: Most modules query online scientific databases. Some local workflows can use downloaded files after setup.

faq.question: Can it process private clinical data?
faq.answer: Use caution. The skill is for bioinformatics guidance and may send queries to external public databases.

faq.question: How should credentials be handled?
faq.answer: Use secure local configuration or environment management. Avoid command-line secrets, shared notebooks, and prompt text.
